name: Chan Chan
info: Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimor kingdom on the arid north coast of Peru, built by the Chimú around 850 CE, and is now an archaeological site of adobe palaces five kilometres west of Trujillo.

facts.founded: Believed to have been constructed around 850 CE by the Chimú; the city was the capital of Chimor from 900 to 1470.
facts.where: At the mouth of the Moche Valley in the coastal desert of northern Peru, in the department of La Libertad, five kilometres west of Trujillo and close to the Pacific Ocean.
facts.known: Capital of the Chimor kingdom; ten walled ciudadelas of adobe; carved reliefs of fish, birds and nets; canal irrigation from the Moche river; Chimú pottery and textiles; conquest by the Incas around 1470; looting by the Spaniards
facts.today: Chan Chan is an archaeological site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 1986, and has been called the largest adobe city in the Americas.

t: The Chimú built Chan Chan around 850 CE as the capital of Chimor, a conquest state on the Peruvian coast, and it held an estimated 40,000 to 60,000 people.
The city rested on canals that carried water from the Moche river, and its rulers lived in ten walled ciudadelas while artisans worked in small rooms that doubled as workshops.
The Incas conquered the Chimú around 1470 and dispersed them, the Spaniards looted the city after Pizarro founded Trujillo in 1535, and excavations began in 1969.
dyk: The Chimú held that the sun created three eggs: gold for the ruler and the elite, silver for the rulers' spouses, and copper for everyone else.
ev: Chan Chan is the capital of the Chimor kingdom from about this year

sections.origins:
Chan Chan lies at the mouth of the Moche Valley, in a particularly arid part of the coastal desert of northern Peru. There is almost no rain, so the main source of fresh water was rivers carrying runoff from the Andes, and that runoff allowed the control of land and water through irrigation systems. Unlike most coastal ruins in Peru, the city stands very close to the Pacific Ocean.

Chan Chan is believed to have been constructed around 850 CE by the Chimú. Chimor, a conquest state, developed from the Chimú culture that established itself along the Peruvian coast around 900 CE, and Chan Chan was its capital from 900 to 1470. At first the city relied on wells about 15 metres deep. A network of canals diverting water from the Moche river was then dug to increase the farmland around it, and once the canals were in place the city had the potential to grow substantially.

The meaning and the language of origin of the name remain unresolved. The place appears as Cauchan in the foundation act of the Trujillo town council of 1536, and the form Chanchan appears in documents in a stable way only from the mid-17th century.
sections.growth:
The city of Chan Chan spanned 20 square kilometres and had a dense urban centre of six square kilometres. It was the capital of Chimor with an estimated population of 40,000 to 60,000 people. The archaeological site is considered the largest adobe city in the Americas.

The canals that made this growth possible could run as long as 20 miles down the Moche valley into the city. Many of the canals to the north were destroyed by a catastrophic flood around 1100 CE, which was the key motivation for the Chimú to refocus their economy on foreign resources rather than on subsistence farming.

Although Chan Chan was an agricultural city, its people were famous for their pottery and textiles, and many craftsmen designed fabrics, pots and ceramics there. The size of the monumental architecture indicates that a large labour force was available. The Huaca Arco Iris, described as the largest adobe monumental complex in South America, is placed chronologically alongside the first structures built at Chan Chan, towards the end of the Middle Horizon in the Central Andes.
sections.rulers:
Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimor kingdom, a conquest state, from 900 to 1470. The coastal society was governed by a powerful ruler called the Chimucapac and was held together by strict control of water and by external threats. The city consisted of ten citadels, which suggests that Chan Chan had ten rulers, and each citadel was built for a ruler or a deity.

Around 1470 the Incas defeated the Chimú and incorporated Chimor into the Inca Empire. The Incas applied what is called the mitma system of ethnic dispersion, which moved Chimú civilians to places the Incas had recently conquered. One account holds that the Incas cut off the canals that fed the city, leaving its crops dying from lack of water, and that the irrigation system was one of the main reasons the Chimú were conquered.

Chan Chan fell into decline after the conquest. Francisco Pizarro founded the Spanish city of Trujillo in 1535, a little over sixty years later, and that city pushed Chan Chan further into the shadows.
sections.life:
Chan Chan had a hierarchical society in which deities and rulers ranked highest and servants lowest. It held nobles, farmers, fishers, traders, servants and many craftsmen. The elite lived in the citadels. The rest of the people lived in small, irregular agglutinated rooms, known as SIARs, which also served as workshops.

The Chimú held that the sun created three eggs, gold for the ruler and the elite, silver for the rulers' spouses, and copper for everyone else. They worshipped the nearby Pacific Ocean, from which most of their food came, and they relied heavily on their irrigation system for crops. The Tschudi compound is believed to have been built in honour of a sea deity whose name in Quingnam is unknown, and a pond in its middle was probably used in religious ceremonies.

The people of Chan Chan supposedly spoke Quingnam, a language that became extinct after the Inca conquest and is poorly documented. No evidence exists for a written system. Anthropologists theorise that they kept records on knotted cords called khipus, as the Incas did, although no artefacts survive to confirm it.
sections.crises:
The first blow to the city's water supply was the catastrophic flood of about 1100 CE, which destroyed many canals to the north. The Chimú responded by turning towards foreign resources rather than subsistence farming.

The Inca conquest around 1470 ended Chan Chan's time as a capital. The Incas dispersed Chimú civilians to other conquered places, and according to one account they cut off the irrigation canals that ran down the Moche valley. After Pizarro founded Trujillo in 1535 the Spaniards looted the city, which was still well known for its riches. A sixteenth-century list of items taken from a burial tomb in Chan Chan records a treasure equivalent to 80,000 pesos of gold.

The adobe buildings continued to suffer afterwards. Many of the city's buildings have been destroyed. Heavy rains, flooding and strong winds erode the structures, and El Niño storms damage the bases of the walls, where humidity leads to salt contamination and plant growth.
sections.legacy:
Chan Chan is now an archaeological site in the department of La Libertad, five kilometres west of Trujillo. Its ten walled ciudadelas housed ceremonial rooms, burial chambers, temples, reservoirs and residences for the Chimú rulers. The walls were adobe brick with a smooth surface carved with birds, fish, small mammals, crabs, turtles and nets, in a realistic and in a more stylised manner. The Tschudi compound had a single entrance and walls up to twelve metres high, wider at the base than at the top, in anticipation of earthquakes.

Michael Moseley and Carol J. Mackey began excavations in 1969, and the work continues under the Peruvian Instituto Nacional de Cultura. A map made by Harvard University in 1974 was the newest until 2017. On 28 November 1986 UNESCO designated Chan Chan a World Heritage Site and placed it on the List of World Heritage in Danger. A conservation master plan was drawn up in 1998. The Italian Mission in Peru has worked at the site since 2002 and has made three-dimensional models of the Tschudi Palace and the Huaca Arco Iris.

Archaeologists have recently given Mochica names to the compounds, although the Chimor spoke Quingnam, which is unrelated to Mochica. This has been criticised as a denial of local history.

summary: Chan Chan, on the desert coast of Peru near Trujillo, was the capital of the Chimor kingdom from about 900 until the Inca conquest around 1470. Its adobe citadels were looted by the Spaniards and are now a World Heritage Site.
notes: Only the city's own article existed; no History article. It is short, so some sections run near the lower length.

START: the article says 'constructed around 850 AD' and, elsewhere, that Chimor was capital 'from 900 to 1470' and that the Chimú culture established itself around 900 CE. I used c. 850 for start and gave both. END 1470 is 'around 1470' (conquest); the article says Chan Chan 'fell into decline', not that it was abandoned.

The article says both that the flood of c. 1100 refocused the economy and that the canals were later cut by the Incas; the Inca irrigation cut-off is attributed ('one account') because the article gives no source.

The article does not say who described or first surveyed the site before 1969; the name Tschudi is not explained. Nothing is claimed about discovery. Spanish looting is told as the article does, with no figure beyond the 80,000 pesos of gold (the article's dollar equivalent was left out).

Left out: tourism (only Tschudi open to visitors), the 2026 mausoleum in the Utzh An complex (a recent find, details thin), the May 2025 vandalism, UAV survey technicalities, the 46 points of critical damage, the claim that it is the 'second' largest adobe city in the world, and the etymology proposals in detail (Urban, Cerrón-Palomino).

Inconsistency: the article says the Tschudi walls were 'up to twelve meters' and elsewhere that the city walls are 50-60 feet (15-18 m); also 'a typical citadel complex is 40 feet tall'. I used only the twelve metres for Tschudi.
The article's 'ten citadels, of which only four have been recovered' and 'ten rulers' is an inference ('suggests'); I kept the hedge.
The 'Tschudi' sea deity and its pond: 'likely'/'believed' hedges kept as 'is believed' and 'probably'.
